Financial planning · Rate timing on declining debt · Visual planning guide

The same average rate can produce different interest costs when the loan balance is shrinking

Reverse two annual interest-rate blocks on a four-year equal-principal loan, compare the shared debt path and different cash payments, and reconcile why their identical average rate does not imply equal cost.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Reverse two annual rate blocks while keeping four equal principal repayments

Interactive planning lab

Total interest: block A first, then B$5,280
Total interest: block B first, then A$4,320
A-first interest less B-first interest$960

Original hypothetical four-year declining-principal loan. Each of four equal one-year periods starts with the shown principal; that year’s annual rate applies to the entire opening balance. Interest is paid in full at year-end, followed by repayment of one quarter of the initial principal. Total payments therefore vary with interest; this is not a level-total-payment amortization or a current lender quote. Block A applies for two years and block B for two years, then their order is reversed. Both cases have the same principal path, term and unweighted average annual rate. No interest is capitalized, and no extra borrowing, prepayment, fees, tax, payment delay or discounting is modeled. Principal repayments use separate household cash and end the balance at zero after year four. The model explains rate timing on a shrinking balance; it does not forecast variable rates, calculate a regulated APR or establish affordability.

The central idea

An interest rate is multiplied by the debt outstanding when it applies. A simple average discards that pairing, so rate timing can change both total interest and the household payment calendar.

01

Keep each rate beside the amount of debt to which it applies

A four-year average interest rate can hide the order in which rates occur. If principal falls during the loan, a high rate in an early year applies to more money than the same high rate near the end. Counting how often each rate appears is therefore insufficient to identify the total dollar interest.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s personal-loan guide explains that borrowing involves principal, interest, payment terms and potentially fees. This illustration keeps those components distinct while using its own simplified repayment rule. It is not a reproduction of a lender’s loan quotation.

The model borrows CAD 24,000 and repays CAD 6,000 of principal at the end of each of four whole years. Each year’s interest is paid separately at the same checkpoint. The amount of principal repaid is fixed, while the total annual payment changes with that year’s interest.

02

Reverse the rate blocks without changing their arithmetic average

Block A has a hypothetical annual rate of 10% and block B has a hypothetical rate of 6%. The A-first sequence uses 10%, 10%, 6% and 6%. The B-first sequence uses 6%, 6%, 10% and 10%.

Each sequence contains two years at each rate, so both have a simple average of 8%. Neither rate is an offer or a forecast. Swapping their order leaves the same four input rates, but changes which rate meets the larger early loan balances.

The principal chart is shared by both sequences. Opening balances for the four interest periods are CAD 24,000, CAD 18,000, CAD 12,000 and CAD 6,000. After the final CAD 6,000 principal repayment, the loan is zero. No unpaid interest is added to the balance, and neither sequence receives a larger repayment simply because its interest bill is lower.

Because principal repayments occur annually, the opening debt remains outstanding throughout each full year. Dividing an annual payment by twelve could suggest a monthly saving allocation, but it would not convert this into a monthly repayment loan. Actual monthly principal reductions would change the interest calculation and need their own schedule.

03

Calculate interest on each year’s opening balance

In the A-first case, the first two interest bills are CAD 2,400 and CAD 1,800. The later 6% rate applies to CAD 12,000 and CAD 6,000, producing CAD 720 and CAD 360. Total interest is CAD 5,280.

In the B-first case, 6% on the larger early balances produces CAD 1,440 and CAD 1,080. The later 10% rate produces CAD 1,200 and CAD 600. Total interest is CAD 4,320. The difference is CAD 960 despite the matching 8% simple average.

The waterfall subtracts the B-first interest from the A-first interest one year at a time. It adds CAD 960 and CAD 720 in the first two years, then subtracts CAD 480 and CAD 240 in the last two. The early additions exceed the later reductions because more principal was outstanding when the early rate difference applied.

04

Add principal back when assessing the household cash calendar

Interest is the borrowing-cost component here, but it is not the full amount leaving the household account. Every annual payment also returns CAD 6,000 of principal. The payment bars include both parts so they can be read as cash requirements.

The A-first annual payments are CAD 8,400, CAD 7,800, CAD 6,720 and CAD 6,360. Their total is CAD 29,280: the original CAD 24,000 principal plus CAD 5,280 interest. The B-first total is CAD 28,320, including the same principal and CAD 4,320 interest.

The shared principal component cancels when comparing total costs, but it still needs funding on every due date. A household cannot reserve only the interest amounts and assume the loan will disappear. This example also does not assume that money saved on an earlier payment is invested, spent, or used for an additional principal repayment. Such choices would change the modeled cash flows.

05

An average rate applied to average-looking debt is another assumption

Using a constant 8% rate on the actual four opening balances would produce CAD 4,800 of interest. That is a third, different rate path. It sits between the two default totals, but it is not equal to either of them. Replacing the original order with an average has changed the calculation.

The four opening balances sum to CAD 60,000 across the four one-year exposures. This does not mean the household borrowed CAD 60,000: the same declining loan is observed repeatedly. Dividing each interest total by that balance sum gives 8.8% and 7.2% respectively, making the different balance weights visible.

Those last percentages are arithmetic summaries for this invented schedule, not regulated APRs, quoted annual borrowing costs or a substitute for valuing the dated payments. For this assumed balance-based interest rule, applying 8% to the full original CAD 24,000 for all four years would ignore the principal repayments entirely. A contract that explicitly uses a flat original-principal basis is a different calculation.

06

Use the rate-pair matrix without turning the scenarios into a forecast

The matrix replaces the two rate blocks while retaining the initial principal and four equal repayments. A positive cell means A-first interest exceeds B-first interest. A negative cell means the reverse. Matching rates produce zero difference, as does a zero initial loan.

The direction follows the pairing. Putting the larger rate first applies it to more principal under this repayment schedule. That is a conditional calculation, rather than a claim about which direction market rates will move. The tool does not let the household choose a future rate path or lock in rates shown only as assumptions.

An actual loan may instead keep total payments level, change payments after a reset, calculate interest daily, charge fees or capitalize unpaid interest. Those terms can change the principal path and require another model. Record the rate basis, outstanding debt and repayment rule together before using a rate average in a budget. The five views isolate that relationship while keeping total interest, principal repayment and affordability as separate planning questions.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All five charts are original hypothetical loan calculations. Four equal annual principal repayments are fixed independently of interest, solely to isolate rate timing. No lender quote, forecast, actual variable-rate repayment structure or regulated APR is calculated. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
